In this lesson you will learn about the computer's motherboard and the major components that are associated with it.
INTRODUCTIONM

The motherboard is sometimes called the heart of the computer because all the components which are needed for the computer to function are either located on the motherboard or are attached to it in some way...

We'll be discussing some of the major components that are located on it, and we'll also discuss some of the different styles of motherboards that have been used and the ones most commonly in use today...
Let's begin the lesson on THE MOTHERBOARD.................................
LESSON MENU
A motherboard is a Printed Circuit Board (PCB) with an array of components attached.
DISCUSSION

The motherboard has either a socket or a slot into which the CPU (Central Processing Unit) is inserted. If the motherboard is the heart of the PC, then the CPU is the brain. It is the single most important chip in the computer.puter..
Modern processors contain millions of transistors, which are etched onto a tiny square of silicon called a die.

The chipset set is a set of chips which provide the interface between the CPU and the rest of the machine. There are two different types of chipset architecture: the North/South Bridge type and the Hub type. Hub type.

The North Bridge is the connection (or bridge) between the main processor bus and the relatively slower AGP and PCI buses, as well as to the system RAM, the South Bridge and the rest of the I/O.......

The South bridge is the connection between the PCI bus and the even-slower ISA bus. It also contains the IDE and USB controllers, as well as the link to the built-in I/O, such as serial and parallel ports, floppy disk controller, and keyboard and mouse interfaces..
Memory Controller Hub (MCH) - This hub takes the place of the North Bridge in providing connection between the processor and memory.
I/O Controller Hub - This hub takes the place of the South Bridge in providing connection to the I/O.
The biggest difference between Bridge and Hub is that the hub architecture uses a dedicated chip as a hub interface instead of using the PCI bus, the way that the Bridge architecture does.

This makes a huge difference in all around performance, because the hub is significantly faster in its performance and it doesn't use any of the PCI bus bandwidth, so that all PCI activity is effectively speeded up.

ROM BIOS - The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) is a set of instructions which tell the CPU how to access the devices that let it communicate with the outside world. It consists of both hardware (ROM chips) and software (device drivers, sometimes called drivers).ers).).

The ROM contains instructions that are hard-wired, i.e. they don't go away when the power is turned off, so they're there and available to be used as soon as power is applied to the machine. These instructions are then used to start up, or boot the machine...
Once these instructions are loaded, the machine knows, among other things, how to talk to its peripherals.

Once it knows that, it can go out, find the operating system software, and load it along with the drivers, which are the software component of the BIOS. Then it's ready to load the application programs..
RAM - Random Access Memory is the computer's working memory. This is where the operating system, application software, and data are kept while the machine is running.
The motherboard contains the sockets or slots where the memory plugs in.

In very old systems, the memory consisted of individual chips which plugged into rows of sockets directly on the motherboard. Most modern systems use memory modules (actually small printed circuit boards with several chips on them) which plug into memory slots....

The old individual chips were called DIPs (Dual In-line Package). They were replaced by SIMMs (Single In-line Memory Module), which have since been superceded by DIMMs (Dual In-line Memory Modules)...
DRAM (Dynamic RAM) is the kind used for the computers main memory. It is very high in density ( a lot of data can fit in a physically small space), but also relatively low speed....
There are two different kinds of RAM found on the motherboard: DRAM and SRAM.
SRAM (Static RAM) is relatively low in density but is very high in speed.ed.

Cache - The CPU runs many times faster than even the fastest DRAM, so in order to allow the CPU to run efficiently, faster SRAM is used to store (or cache) frequently-used instructions and data. Cache is special area of memory reserved to hold data and instructions recently accessed from another location.
Most systems these days use two levels of cache: Level 1 (L1) and Level 2 (L2).

L1 cache is part of the same die as the main processor itself. Since it's on the same die, the access time is very small, and since it's very fast RAM to begin with, it enables the CPU to function at full speed...
This is especially important these days, with CPU speeds on the rough order of a thousand times as high as they were in the first personal computers.

L2 cache originally resided on the motherboard, immediately adjacent to the main processor socket. It was a larger cache than the L1, but it was slower since it could only send its data out at motherboard speeds...
These days it is usually located in the chip with the main processor and the L1 cache, which enables systems to run even faster.

I/O Ports - There are several I/O (input/output) ports which are an essential part of an operating computer. These are the connections between the computer and the rest of the world.

Serial port - the serial port is used primarily for communication with other computers, but it can also be used for connection to certain printers and plotters, instrumentation, and various types of control devices.

Parallel port - The parallel port was originally the exclusive purpose of sending data to the printer, but contemporary versions have been enhanced to allow it to perform additional functions, such as connection to certain types of LANs, disks, cameras, and so on.ameras, and so on.

Keyboard - older systems used a 5-pin DIN socket, but most newer systems use either the 6-pin mini-DIN socket (usually called a PS/2 port) or a USB connector. Some systems use an infrared port, called an IrDA (for Infrared Data)..
PS/2 - the PS/2 port uses a 6-pin mini-DIN socket. It was originally developed for the IBM PS/2 system, but is used on newer systems for keyboards, mice, and other input and pointing devices.

Buses - A bus is a common electrical pathway across which data can travel within a computer. All of the various components on the motherboard communicate across buses of one sort or another. The buses themselves are controlled by the chipset..

Processor Bus - this is the highest speed bus in the computer. It is the bus that is used to pass data back and forth between the processor and the cache memory, and between the processor and the North Bridge of the chipset..

Local Bus - The local bus directly connects to the processor and shares its full speed and data transfer width (that is, a 64-bit processor will have a 64-bit local bus instead of a 32- or 16-bit bus). Most commonly it is used to support cache RAM and high speed graphics.....
The chipset then passes the data to and from the main system memory, to other buses, or to the South Bridge.
PCI Bus - this bus is generated by the North Bridge and is used to communicate with the I/O cards in the PCI slots and with the South Bridge.

The AGP bus is the specialized bus is used to carry data for the Accelerated Graphics Port. It is based on PCI but includes some additional signals and doesn't support any other components; it is completely independent of the PCI bus.

The Memory bus is used exclusively to transfer data between the RAM and the CPU. It is attached to the chipset North Bridge or the Memory Control Hub, depending on the type of architecture used on the motherboard.rboard..

The ISA bus is the oldest of the major types of I/O buses. ISA stands for Industry Standard Architecture, and although the bus and adapter cards have been far surpassed by newer buses and cards, there are still some in use today.ay..
Although they lack the speed of more modern components, they are still capable of providing useful I/O, especially in situations where very high speeds aren't really necessary.

The MCA bus was developed by IBM as a replacement for the ISA bus, the Micro Channel Architecture Bus was faster and more powerful than ISA and far easier to set up and use: there are no switches or jumpers involved whatsoever.
The only reason that MCA didn't take the industry by storm was that IBM decided that they wanted to receive royalties for its use, so they kept it as a proprietary system.
The licensing agreements included retroactive royalties for the ISA bus as well. This did not go over well; industry ignored the new bus rather than pay the licensing fees.

The EISA Bus (Extended Industry Standard Architecture) was developed in response to IBM's introduction of the MCA bus. Originally developed by Compaq, it was released as an open standard in order to ensure that vendors would support it..

Unfortunately, it just never caught on and few adapter cards were ever developed. Most of the cards that were produced were disk array and server network cards, so there was a niche market, but that was all...

One of the most important features of the new bus was the ability of the slot to accommodate either the older ISA cards or the newer EISA cards, and most EISA slots ended up being used with older ISA cards...
The USB (Universal Serial Bus) is becoming the most popular expansion bus ever invented. USB version 1.x offers speeds of up to 12 Mbits/second, and version 2.x can go as high as 480 Mbits/second..

USB offers a long list of improvements over existing expansion buses. For instance, the bus can include up to 127 different devices simultaneously, although this bandwidth is shared among all the peripherals connected...

For another thing, it acts to consolidate all I/O devices, so many different kinds of devices can be connected, such as disk drives, mice and other pointing devices, keyboards, scanners, printers, and so on...

The peripherals are hot-swappable, meaning they can be connected or disconnected while the system and the peripheral are both powered on, without any need to restart. They are automatically recognized and configured as soon as they are physically connected.onnected..

They all share the same set of system resources; under any previous bus architecture they would each require a separate share of the system's resources. They also don't require separate slots on the motherboard. In fact, some act as hubs, providing connection points for other peripherals...
IEEE-1394 - this bus, known as either FireWire or i.Link, was originally developed by Apple Computer and was turned over to the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers in late 1995.

The original version offered connectivity of 100, 200, or 400 Mbits per second. It is expected that second-generation standards will reach the gigabit range. Because of the enormously fast transfer rates, it has gained popularity for use with digital video and multimedia...
The PCMCIA (PC-Card) bus standard is maintained by the Personal Computer Memory Card International Association and is primarily aimed at the portable computing arena.na.

PC cards are about the size of a credit card and are intended to fit into a small slot on a laptop or notebook computer in order to add expansion capabilities to computers which, by design, have no extra room inside for expansion...
They can be used to expand memory, to add fax/modem capability, network interface adapters, disk drive adapters, or whatever is needed.

The last motherboard component to mention is the battery. The battery provides the power to maintain the system configuration settings which are kept in non-volatile memory, known as NVRAM, and to maintain the system clock, called the Real Time Clock.ime Clock..

The NVRAM keeps track of such things as the size and type of hard disk and Plug-and-Play information necessary for the system to start up, but that can't be efficiently stored in the ROM BIOS because of the need to occasionally change the information..y change the information.

The NVRAM is frequently referred to as the CMOS, which stands for Complimentary Metal Oxide Semiconductor. It is named for the material used in the construction of the chip itself.nd the battery is often referred to as the CMOS battery.
The battery is often referred to as the CMOS battery. Lithium batteries are generally used because of their long life.w power-consumption situation..n situation.

Some systems use a chip that has the battery built in. The chip is socketed so that it can be replaced in the event of failure, but the normal life expectancy of the batteries used in these chips is at least ten years or more - longer than the life expectancy of the computer itself..

The motherboard is the main printed circuit board in an electronic device, particularly a computer. It's called a motherboard because it contains sockets (called slots) that accept additional circuit boards, known as daughter-boards.
DISCUSSION

The reason that the motherboard is sometimes referred to as the heart of the personal computer is because all of the basic circuitry and components required for a PC to function are either contained on the motherboard or attached to it in some way...
The motherboard typically contains the CPU, the buses, memory slots, expansion slots, I/O ports, and peripheral controllers.
The motherboard may also be referred to as the main board, system board, or logic board. Regardless of what you call it, it is the central component that ties together everything in the PC.PC..
A number of factors go into determining which motherboard is used:
RAM - type, number of slots, and maximum amount
Proprietary video, memory, or peripheral device controllersssdevice controllers

The motherboard's general size, layout, and component placement make up what is known as the form factor. The example shown is an ATX board, which is the most common form factor, but there are several other standard dimensions available...

Advances in computer technology are reflected in advances in motherboard design. Let's compare some of the various motherboard configurations and their effects on system compatibility and capabilities...

The ATX form factor corrects some design flaws of the AT form factor, such as conflicts in component location, and makes allowances for upgrades to incorporate newer technologies.
The ATX form factor was designed to address four areas of improvement:
Better support for current and future processor technology
Better support for current and future I/O
The ATX motherboard requires a specific case and power supply design. It is similar to a Baby AT rotated 90 degrees, with a new mounting configuration and connector for the power supply.

The processor is relocated away from the expansion slots, allowing them to hold full-length add-in cards (adapters, expansion cards, etc.). With the longer side of the board facing the rear panel, the layout allows for more expansion slots...
The original ATX power supply pulled air into of the chassis and pushed it throughout the chassis and across the processor, rather than exhausteing air out of the chassis..

This design innovation didn't work out as planned, because the air flow was already warmed by its trip through the power supply before it ever got near the main processor. Newer power supplies have gone back to the older technique of exhausting the air instead of pulling it in..n.
The ATX standard also specifies a single power supply connector for the motherboard. The connector is keyed and shrouded to prevent accidental reversal or misalignment..
This is a relief for the average end user, who previously had to worry about interchanging the power supply connectors and subsequently damaging the motherboard.
One Power Connector providing + 3V, + 5V + 12V, and ground. ground....ll not fit into a slimline case.

The connector also has pins for supplying +3.3 V to the motherboard, which means that ATX motherboards don't require built-in voltage regulators, eliminating one possible source of component failure...

The MicroATX developed as a natural evolution of the ATX form factor to address new market trends and technologies, the microATX supports:::
The transition to newer processor technologies.
Smaller motherboard size (with fewer expansion slots available).
The FlexATX is derived from the microATX design. It offers the opportunity for system developers to be creative with new PC designs..designs.
Supports current socketed processor technologies (no Slot 1, Slot A, ect.).
FlexATX was designed to allow flexibility for customized case and board designs to be manufactured, such as all-in-one computing devices, LCD-personal computers or standard desktop systems...
The NLX form factor is a new low-profile motherboard standard, introduced by Intel in 1999 to replace the LPX. It is similar to the LPX, but includes several improvements.

It supports motherboard dimensions of 8.0" - 9.0" x 10.0"- 13.6" and segregates taller components on the left, allowing expansion slots (which are located on a riser card at the right edge of the motherboard) to hold full-length add-in cards.
It was designed for the Pentium II CPU as well as future (socketed) processors, and it supports AGP high performance graphics, Universal Serial Bus, and tall memory technologies (DIMMs)...

It allows easier access to internal components, with improved thermal and clearance issues regarding CPU. Also, the I/O connectors are stacked single and double high at the back of the motherboard to support more connectors...

A new, convenient feature is the Tool-less architecture, which allows removal without the use of tools. In this unique set-up, the riser card (normally a daughter card) is fastened to the chassis, while the motherboard slides into a slot at the bottom of the riser...
With the covers off, the motherboard slides out the side of the chassis while the riser card and the expansion cards stay put..

NLX is an open specification, intended for widespread use in many types of systems, and several major PC vendors have worked jointly to define it and to incorporate flexibility to accommodate the best designs for current and future PCs...
High-capacity power supplies (up to 850 W).
Easy access to memory and expansion slots.
Flex Slot I/O cards (double-wide PCI cards) - allows normal I/O to be moved further from the main processor, chipset, and RAM to help minimize EMI (electromagnetic interference).
The last new form factor that we'll examine is the WTX board. It was developed primarily for mid-range workstations, not for lower-end stand-alone personal computers..ters.
Up to 14" wide by up to 16.75" long (no mimimums specified).
Designed to support future processor, graphics, and memory technologies, (32-and 64-bit).
Tower chassis or rackmount capabilities..

Unlike other standards, WTX doesn't physically define the size and shape of the board. Instead, it specifies that the motherboard interfaces with the chassis via a standardized mounting adapter, which must be supplied with the motherboard.
The WTX standard also defines some required features of the chassis itself, such as swing-out doors and slide-out drawers for access to internal components.
